ai.summary: Researchers interviewed 15 international students at a London university about sexually transmitted infection testing. They found that language gaps, stigma, and distant services made testing harder, while confidentiality, trust in professionals, and knowing about free, easy testing made it easier.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding these barriers helps universities and health services design better sexual health support for students from diverse backgrounds.
ai.life_skill: Find out where free, confidential STI testing is available near your university or home.
ai.fact: Confidentiality and trust in health professionals can encourage people to get tested for sexually transmitted infections.

quiz.question: What did the researchers identify as the main social barrier to STI testing among the students interviewed?
quiz.answer: Anticipated judgement and stigma were the main social opportunity barriers to testing.

ai.caveat: This is a small preprint from one London university that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the results may not apply more widely.

items.title: Modular functional brain network organization contributes to training-related changes in task switching in children

ai.headline: Children with more modular brain networks before training improved faster at task switching.
ai.summary: Researchers studied 87 children aged 8 to 11 during nine weeks of task-switching training. More modular brain networks before training were linked to higher accuracy and faster early gains in combined speed-accuracy scores.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that baseline brain network organisation may help explain why some people benefit more from cognitive training than others.
ai.fact: More modular organisation of functional brain networks before training was linked to higher task-switching accuracy and faster early improvement in children aged 8 to 11.

quiz.question: What was linked to faster early improvements in children's task-switching training?
quiz.answer: More modular organisation of functional brain networks before training was linked to faster early improvements.

ai.caveat: The findings are from a single preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the observational design cannot prove that modularity causes the faster improvement.

items.title: AI evaluators favor job applications written by certain AI models, independent of candidate quality

ai.headline: AI hiring tools may reject good candidates simply because they used a different AI to write their cover letter.
ai.summary: This preprint tested how AI evaluators rate job applications written by various AI models. It found that evaluators consistently favour applications from specific models and their own outputs, regardless of the candidate's actual qualifications.
ai.why_it_matters: If you use AI to help with job applications, the specific tool you choose could unfairly disadvantage you compared to others using different tools.
ai.life_skill: Check if your employer uses AI screening and consider how your choice of writing tool might affect the outcome.
ai.fact: AI evaluators show a consistent preference hierarchy for certain writer models, often favouring their own outputs over others.

quiz.question: Did the study find that AI evaluators judged candidates based on their actual qualifications?
quiz.answer: No, the study found that evaluators favoured specific AI models and their own outputs independently of candidate quality.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are not yet confirmed by the scientific community.

items.title: HOW GUT MICROBIOTA MAY MEDIATE THE ANTI-SEIZURE EFFECTS OF KETOGENIC DIET IN PEDIATRIC DRUG-RESISTANT EPILEPSY: A NARRATIVE REVIEW

ai.headline: Gut bacteria may help the ketogenic diet reduce seizures in children with drug-resistant epilepsy.
ai.summary: This narrative review examines how the ketogenic diet (KD) works for pediatric drug-resistant epilepsy. It suggests that beyond ketones, specific gut bacteria produce chemicals that calm brain activity, similar to how some seizure medications work.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that what we eat can change our gut bacteria, which in turn can influence how our brain functions and responds to treatment.
ai.life_skill: Notice that your diet can influence your gut health, which is linked to overall well-being.
ai.fact: Specific gut bacteria, such as Akkermansia muciniphila, are required for the ketogenic diet to effectively reduce seizures in animal models.

quiz.question: According to the review, how might gut bacteria help the ketogenic diet work?
quiz.answer: They produce short-chain fatty acids that modulate the balance of GABA and glutamate in the hippocampus.

ai.caveat: This is a narrative review, not a systematic one, and the mechanistic evidence for the gut-brain link is primarily from preclinical (animal) studies rather than direct human trials.

items.title: The Workings of Social Fields: Poverty, Capital, and Symbolic Violence across Five Domains

ai.headline: Having useful skills and qualifications does not guarantee a livelihood because others control how they are valued and used.
ai.summary: The paper compares six analyses of Dutch interviews across employment, welfare, informal exchange, neighbourhood relations and debt management. It finds that recognition of a resource can coexist with blocked access, and that people may keep only part of what a resource produces because control over valuation, access and benefits is split between different actors.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows why immediate help, personal freedom and lasting financial improvement are different things that should not be confused when tackling poverty.
ai.life_skill: Notice who decides whether your skills or connections actually count in a given situation, not just whether they are recognised.
ai.fact: Recognition of a skill or resource can exist at the same time as blocked access to using it.

quiz.question: What can coexist with blocked access to a resource, according to the paper?
quiz.answer: Recognition of the resource can coexist with blocked access to using it.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed and synthesises existing interview analyses rather than presenting new evidence.

items.title: Saving for the Machines -- by Jesús Fernández-Villaverde

ai.headline: Automation growth depends on capital accumulation
ai.summary: The study examined how automation affects economic growth, finding that capital accumulation plays a crucial role in determining the size of the growth boom. The research used a standard task model to analyze the impact of automation on growth and wages. The results showed that a fixed saving rate can lead to slower growth, while an optimal saving rate can deliver higher growth rates.
ai.why_it_matters: This research matters because it suggests that slow economic growth might be due to insufficient capital accumulation rather than a technological bottleneck, which has implications for economic policy and decision-making.
ai.life_skill: Try to understand the importance of saving and investing in a rapidly changing technological landscape.
ai.fact: The same technology path can deliver different growth rates depending on the saving rate.

quiz.question: What can affect the size of the growth boom associated with automation?
quiz.answer: Capital accumulation can affect the size of the growth boom associated with automation.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings should be interpreted with caution.

items.title: Reducing Stroke Risk in African-American Men

ai.headline: A six-month trial tested a targeted management intervention for African-American men after stroke or TIA.
ai.summary: The study compared a TEAM intervention with a wait-list control in 160 African-American men who had a stroke or transient ischaemic attack in the past five years. It was a randomised controlled trial, but the abstract does not report what the intervention involved or what results were found.
ai.why_it_matters: Stroke prevention matters because it can reduce serious illness and death in a group known to face higher stroke risk.

quiz.question: What type of study compared TEAM with a wait-list control?
quiz.answer: It was a six-month prospective randomised controlled trial.

ai.caveat: The abstract gives no results, so it is not possible to say whether the intervention worked.

items.title: Restricting candy may increase kids' urge to overeat, research suggests

ai.headline: Restricting candy may increase children's urge to overeat it, research suggests.
ai.summary: The article discusses research suggesting that restricting candy may increase children's urge to overeat it. It focuses on how parents handle negotiations around candy consumption after holidays and events.
ai.why_it_matters: It highlights how common parenting approaches to sweets might unintentionally affect children's eating behaviour.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether restricting certain foods makes you or others want them more.
ai.fact: Restricting candy may increase children's urge to overeat it.

quiz.question: What does the research suggest happens when candy is restricted?
quiz.answer: It may increase children's urge to overeat it.

ai.caveat: This is a news report, not the original research, so the study design and findings cannot be verified from the abstract alone.

items.title: Five overlooked steps to identify new epidemics, fast

ai.headline: Current epidemic tracking fails when diseases cause unusual or unexpected symptoms.
ai.summary: This commentary highlights a major limitation in current measures for tracking emerging epidemics. It notes that these systems do not work effectively if a disease presents with unusual or unexpected symptoms.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding this gap helps explain why some new health threats might be missed or delayed in detection by public health systems.
ai.life_skill: Notice that standard health alerts might miss diseases with unusual symptoms, so stay open to new information from official sources.
ai.fact: Current epidemic tracking measures have a key limitation regarding diseases with unusual or unexpected symptoms.

quiz.question: What is a key limitation of current epidemic tracking measures mentioned in the text?
quiz.answer: They don’t work if the disease causes unusual or unexpected symptoms.

ai.caveat: This is a commentary identifying a limitation, not a study providing new data or testing a solution.

ai.summary: This news report describes how Democrats hope to win voters by focusing on cuts to health-care programmes ahead of the US midterm elections.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how health-care spending can become a major political issue that affects everyday voters.
ai.life_skill: Check how political parties plan to fund health-care programmes before voting.
ai.fact: Democrats hope to win voters’ support by focusing on cuts to health-care programmes.

quiz.answer: They hope to focus on cuts to health-care programmes.

items.title: Collective human metabolism produces 2 billion metric tons of CO₂ a year, global study estimates

ai.headline: Human breathing released an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons of CO₂ in 2015, up 74% since 1985.
ai.summary: Researchers estimated the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism as bodies convert food into energy. They found it rose by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons a year.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how human activity fits into the global carbon cycle and where carbon comes from and goes.
ai.life_skill: Notice how everyday activities like eating and moving connect to the wider environment.
ai.fact: Human metabolism produced an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons of CO₂ in 2015.

quiz.question: By what percentage did CO₂ from human metabolism rise between 1985 and 2015?
quiz.answer: It rose by 74%.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about an estimate, not the full peer-reviewed study, so the figures and methods cannot be checked here.

items.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F

ai.headline: Some metals stay flexible at ultra-low temperatures by reorganising their internal structure instead of cracking.
ai.summary: Researchers studied two experimental alloys at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), where similar materials usually become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, the alloys reorganised their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain how materials might behave in extreme cold, which could matter for future technologies such as space exploration or cryogenic engineering.
ai.fact: Certain alloys can reorganise their internal structure to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F).

quiz.question: What did the two experimental alloys do at -253°C instead of cracking?
quiz.answer: They reorganised their internal structures to absorb stress and remain flexible.

ai.caveat: This is a news report of a discovery, not a peer-reviewed study, so the details and claims have not been independently verified.

items.title: Outcomes and organ protection effects of perioperative precision venous access management strategies in patients undergoing complex hepatobiliary, pancreatic, splenic and abdominal great vascular surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

ai.headline: Precision venous access management may reduce kidney injury and pancreatic fistula after major abdominal surgery.
ai.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis combined 14 studies with 2,158 adults undergoing complex liver, pancreas, spleen, or major blood vessel surgery. It found that precision venous access management—using advanced monitoring, algorithm-guided therapy, and specialised access—was linked to lower rates of acute kidney injury and clinically relevant pancreatic fistula, fewer overall complications, and shorter hospital stays compared with standard care.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how tailored fluid and monitoring strategies during high-risk surgery might help protect organs and support recovery.
ai.life_skill: Ask your surgical team how your fluids and circulation will be monitored before and after major surgery.
ai.fact: The review included randomised controlled trials and prospective cohort studies comparing precision venous access management with standard treatment.

quiz.question: What did the review find about precision venous access management and acute kidney injury?
quiz.answer: It was linked to a significantly lower incidence of acute kidney injury compared with standard care.

ai.caveat: The included studies varied in design and some were prospective cohorts rather than randomised trials, so the results show a link rather than definitive proof.

items.title: Organizational trust in the workplace: explainable machine learning evidence from Ecuadorian workers

ai.headline: Job satisfaction, cynicism and workplace climate help predict high trust among Ecuadorian workers.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 899 workers in Ecuador about trust in their supervisor and organisation, along with cynicism, climate, satisfaction and personal characteristics. Machine-learning models found satisfaction, cynicism and climate were the most useful predictors, though job satisfaction alone performed almost as well as the full set.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how workplace feelings and environment are linked to whether employees trust their organisation, which can affect daily working life.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether you feel satisfied with your job, cynical about your organisation, and positive about your workplace climate, as these are linked to trust.
ai.fact: In this study, high organisational trust was defined as a mean score of at least 5.0 on a 12-item inventory measuring trust in the immediate supervisor and the organisation.

quiz.question: Which predictor group performed almost as well as the combined set of satisfaction, cynicism and climate?
quiz.answer: Job satisfaction alone reached a mean nested ROC-AUC of 0.843, close to the combined framework’s 0.875.

ai.caveat: This was a non-experimental cross-sectional survey using a convenience sample from Ecuador, so it shows links rather than proof of cause and effect and may not apply elsewhere.

items.title: Exchange Of Instrumental Support Between Grandparents And Grandchildren In Sengerema District, Tanzania
items.venue: International journal of social sciences and humanities review

ai.headline: Grandparents and grandchildren in Tanzania help each other with daily tasks in a flexible, changing way.
ai.summary: A small qualitative study in Sengerema District, Tanzania, explored practical support exchanged between grandparents and grandchildren through interviews, focus groups and observation. Grandparents provided food, clothing, shelter, healthcare, education costs, money, supervision and personal care, while grandchildren helped with farming, fetching water, cooking, cleaning, washing, animal care, errands and physically demanding tasks.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how different generations can share everyday responsibilities to keep households running and support family wellbeing.
ai.life_skill: Notice what practical help you give and receive from older or younger family members, and appreciate that it can change over time.
ai.fact: Instrumental support between grandparents and grandchildren can include basic needs, farming, financial help, childcare and household chores.

quiz.question: What kind of support did grandparents and grandchildren exchange in the study?
quiz.answer: They exchanged practical, material and everyday household help such as food, farming, childcare, cooking, cleaning and errands.

ai.caveat: The findings come from a very small number of participants in one Tanzanian district, so they may not apply elsewhere.

items.title: Modeling the Psychosocial Determinants of Problematic Social Media Use Risk Among High School Students Using Artificial Neural Networks

ai.headline: Academic expectation stress was the strongest predictor of problematic social media use risk among high school students in this model.
ai.summary: Researchers used an artificial neural network and logistic regression to study 899 high school students, looking at academic expectation stress, loneliness, mobile device ownership, and physical activity as predictors of problematic social media use risk. Academic expectation stress had the highest predictive importance, followed by loneliness, mobile device ownership, and physical activity level.
ai.why_it_matters: It highlights which psychosocial factors may be most closely linked to problematic social media use risk in adolescents, helping to understand where support might be focused.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether school-related pressure coincides with increased social media use, and consider talking to a trusted adult or counsellor if it feels hard to manage.
ai.fact: Academic expectation stress had the highest normalized importance (100%) among the four factors studied for predicting problematic social media use risk.

quiz.question: Which factor had the highest normalized importance in predicting problematic social media use risk?
quiz.answer: Academic expectation stress had the highest normalized importance at 100%.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and the findings come from a single observational dataset, so they cannot prove causation.

items.title: The consequences of changes in exercise habits on work engagement and presenteeism: Evidence from an event-study analysis using Japanese longitudinal data
items.venue: Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health

ai.headline: Starting exercise is linked to higher work engagement, while quitting is linked to lower engagement; neither is linked to presenteeism.
ai.summary: Researchers followed over 6,500 Japanese employees across four survey waves to see how starting or stopping exercise habits related to work engagement and presenteeism. Starting exercise was positively associated with work engagement, while quitting was negatively associated with it. Neither starting nor quitting exercise showed a significant association with presenteeism.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that building an exercise habit may support psychological engagement at work, even if it does not clearly improve measured productivity.
ai.life_skill: Try keeping a regular exercise habit rather than focusing only on starting one, since stopping was linked to lower work engagement.
ai.fact: Starting exercise was associated with work engagement over longer follow-up waves than quitting exercise.

quiz.question: What was the association between starting exercise and presenteeism according to the study?
quiz.answer: Starting exercise showed no significant association with presenteeism.

ai.caveat: As an observational study using self-reported survey data, it cannot prove that exercise caused changes in work engagement.

items.title: Prevalence and Sociodemographic Correlates of Depression and Thoughts of Self-Harm Among Adolescents in Five Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Evidence from the Demographic and Health Survey Program

ai.headline: About one in fourteen adolescents in five low- and middle-income countries reported thoughts of death or self-harm, with girls more affected than boys.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed survey data from 16,269 adolescents aged 15-19 in Bangladesh, Lesotho, Mozambique, Nepal and Zambia. Probable depression affected 3.9%, while thoughts of death or self-harm affected 7.0%; girls had higher rates than boys for both.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that thoughts of death or self-harm are not rare among adolescents in these settings, especially girls, so families and communities should be alert to signs of distress.
ai.life_skill: Notice if a friend or family member seems withdrawn, hopeless or talks about death, and encourage them to speak with a trusted adult or a qualified mental health professional.
ai.fact: In this study, probable depression was defined as a PHQ-9 score of 10 or higher, and thoughts of death or self-harm as any endorsement of PHQ-9 item 9.
ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, and its cross-sectional design cannot show causes; PHQ-9 validation and measurement invariance across countries were also lacking.

items.title: DCAF: Unifying Data Validity, Evaluation Validity and Predictive Modeling for Single-cell Perturbation Simulation

ai.headline: A new computer framework improves predictions of how single cells respond to genetic changes.
ai.summary: The study introduces DCAF, a framework that reconstructs cell states before and after genetic perturbation, evaluates prediction errors more sensitively, and models gene regulation. It outperformed existing deep-learning and simple baseline methods across several tests, including adult mouse brain data.
ai.why_it_matters: Better cell-response simulations could speed up understanding of disease and the discovery of new treatments.
ai.fact: DCAF is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed.

quiz.question: What does DCAF aim to improve?
quiz.answer: It aims to improve the simulation of how single cells respond to genetic perturbations.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, so its findings are preliminary.
